pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10 (META). Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing and rounding whole numbers to 1,000,000 — e.g. 'largest six-digit number whose digits sum to 15', round a stadium capacity for a headline, order five city populations and find a range. Applying the whole Year-5 place-value toolkit flexibly and in context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'solve number problems and practical problems that involve all of the above [place value to 1,000,000]'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT / 4.OA multi-step problem-solving with multi-digit numbers, rounding for reasonableness.
• Operational details — Pose rich, multi-step and real-context problems (populations, distances, money, digit-constraint puzzles) that reward choosing among reading, comparing, ordering, rounding and place-value reasoning. Model with number lines, bar models, place-value charts; require justification and appropriate accuracy. Include 'construct a number' puzzles that exercise place value creatively.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): solves a one-step large-number problem with a model. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): solves multi-step problems in context, choosing and explaining the strategy. Tier C (age 10, extending): tackles digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and selects appropriate accuracy.
bestPractices: Pose rich, real-context, multi-step problems (populations, distances, budgets) plus digit-constraint puzzles.
Provide the full toolkit (number line, bar model, chart) and require the child to choose and justify a strategy.
Use rounding to estimate and check reasonableness; choose appropriate accuracy for the context.
Include 'build the largest/smallest number with these constraints' tasks to exercise place value creatively.
Externalise reasoning (think-aloud then child-explains) so strategy choice becomes deliberate.
commonMisconceptions: Applying a memorised procedure without checking it fits.
Rounding at the wrong stage / to unhelpful accuracy.
Ordering/comparing errors with multi-zero or mixed-length numbers.
In digit-constraint puzzles, ignoring the place-value impact of digit position.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: solve multi-step number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000. Learners apply the full place-value toolkit flexibly in context (populations, stadium capacities, distances, budgets) and tackle digit-constraint puzzles such as building the largest number with a given digit sum. The central insight is that place value drives strategy: to maximise a number you load the biggest digits into the highest-value places first. Rounding, ordering and estimation are chosen deliberately to fit each problem and checked for reasonableness.

activities.title: Build the largest number: a digit-constraint puzzle
feedback: If a learner spreads the sum evenly or fills low places (e.g. 333,330, which sums to 15, or 111,138, which also sums to 15), the number is not maximised: compare it against 960,000 column by column. A 9 in the hundred-thousands place beats any arrangement with a smaller leading digit, so the leading place dominates.
If the digits no longer sum to 15, recount the chosen digits before judging size — any counterexample used here must itself sum to 15.
Prompt: 'Why put the 9 in the hundred-thousands place and not in the ones?' to surface that the leftmost place carries the most value.
activities.rationale: A constructive, manipulable puzzle lets children test arrangements, see the value update, and work toward the place-value principle rather than guess. Arranging movable digit-tiles into a chart and comparing candidates can make the strategy explicit; this is a proposed design, not a claim that only this format can teach it.
sourceClaims: Digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and strategy-selection deepen place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Take the task: 'Make the LARGEST six-digit number whose digits add up to 15.'
Arrange digit choices into a six-column place-value chart (hundred-thousands down to ones) and write the value they build.
Compare two of their own candidate numbers place by place, starting from the highest place, and decide which is larger and why.
State the rule they discovered in their own words: to make a number as large as possible, put the biggest digits in the highest-value places first.
Verify the digits still sum to 15 after arranging them (9 + 6 = 15, then zeros gives 960,000).
activities.intendedInsight: Magnitude is controlled by the highest-value places, so maximising a number means front-loading the biggest digits into the leftmost columns while respecting the digit-sum constraint.

activities.title: Round in context for a headline
feedback: If a learner rounds 67,450 up to 68,000, they may be rounding in steps (the 5 tens lift 67,450 to 67,500, then that rounds up to 68,000) or treating the tens digit 5 as the decider: isolate the decider. For nearest thousand, look at the hundreds digit — 4 is less than 5, so round down.
Use the number line: 67,450 sits left of the midpoint 67,500, so it is nearer 67,000.
Prompt: 'Is 67,450 nearer 67,000 or 68,000? How do you know?'
activities.rationale: Rounding errors in context often come from attending to the wrong digit or to the full tail. Naming the deciding digit and anchoring on a number line targets this directly.
sourceClaims: Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: Take a real-context item: 'A stadium holds 67,450 people — round it to the nearest thousand for a news headline.'
Identify the deciding digit for 'nearest thousand' (the hundreds digit) before rounding.
Place 67,450 on a number line between 67,000 and 68,000 and judge which it is nearer.
Give the rounded answer (67,000) and justify it from the deciding digit (the hundreds digit, 4), not by rounding in steps from the tens digit (67,450 → 67,500 → 68,000).
Explain in a sentence why 450 keeps the thousands the same (rounds DOWN to 67,000).
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding to a named place depends on the single deciding digit immediately to the right of that place; here the hundreds digit is 4, which is below 5, so the thousands stay the same.

activities.title: Order populations and find the range
feedback: If a learner orders by the first visible digit (e.g. treating 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 as equal or mis-ordering them because each starts with 9), line the numbers up right-aligned in columns and compare starting from the highest place.
Prompt: 'Order 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 — what do you compare first?' to make column alignment the deciding move.
After finding the range, compare the exact difference to a rounded estimate to catch slips.
activities.rationale: Multi-zero and mixed-length numbers are a classic source of comparison errors; explicit column alignment and highest-place-first comparison address the misconception.
learnerActions: Take five city populations (mixed-length numbers, some with internal zeros) and right-align them by place-value column.
Compare from the highest place downward to order them from smallest to largest.
Order the trio 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 as a focused check, saying which place you compare first.
Find the range by subtracting the smallest from the largest and sense-check the answer against a rounded estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct ordering comes from aligning place-value columns and comparing from the highest place down. For whole numbers, more digits means a larger number, but when numbers have the same number of digits you must compare place by place, not just look at the first visible digit.

activities.title: Choose and justify the strategy (think-aloud)
feedback: If a learner applies a memorised procedure without checking it fits the question, ask them to name the tool and why before computing.
If an answer is wildly off a rounded estimate, treat the mismatch as a signal to recheck rather than to accept the computation.
Naming the strategy after solving (e.g. 'I rounded to estimate, then compared from the highest place') can reinforce transfer.
activities.rationale: This is a META problem-solving topic: externalising reasoning (think-aloud, then child-explains) and estimation-checking support flexible strategy selection. A spoken dialogue and a worked anchor example are useful supplements for eliciting reasoning, not the sole route.
sourceClaims: Digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and strategy-selection deepen place-value problem solving.
Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: For each problem, first answer 'which tool fits?' — number line, bar model, place-value chart, or digit arrangement — before solving.
Hear or read a worked example thought aloud, then re-solve a similar problem explaining each decision.
Estimate first by rounding, then compute the exact answer, and check the exact answer against the estimate.
Discuss with a partner or respond to prompts such as 'how did you decide?' to make the strategy deliberate.
activities.intendedInsight: In multi-step problems the hard part is choosing which place-value tool to use and checking reasonableness; making the choice explicit and estimating first turns strategy into a deliberate repertoire.

constraints: Multi-step and context problems can be assessed with fixed-response items (best-estimate choices, largest-number choices, estimate-then-check sliders, fill-in-the-blank), but recognition-only items do not themselves elicit the independent construction that the digit-building puzzle requires; use a construction task for the maximising strategy.
A worked, tapped-through example (e.g. a solved population-range problem) is a reference anchor, not varied practice; pair it with problems the learner solves themselves.

A live-updating value display and movable digit-tiles are optional supports that make the place-value mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not mandatory mechanisms, and the same insight can be reached on paper with a drawn chart.
For this abstract/contextual numeric reasoning there is little spatial payoff, so 3D manipulation adds little here; prefer number lines, bar models and place-value charts.
Any 'spread evenly / fills low places' counterexample used with the digit-sum-15 task must itself sum to 15 (e.g. 333,330 or 111,138); do not use 333,300, which sums to 12.

Tier expectations: emerging learners solve a one-step large-number problem with a model; secure learners solve multi-step context problems choosing and explaining a strategy; extending learners tackle digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and select appropriate accuracy.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original-row arithmetic error corrected: the error pattern cited '333,300' as a number summing to 15, but 333,300 sums to 12. Replaced with 333,330 (sums to 15) in the learner-facing activity; the original figure is kept only here and in preservationAudit.uncertain.

Self-audit of worked values: the largest six-digit number with digit sum 15 is 960,000 (9+6=15, remaining places 0) — the maximum by front-loading. 67,450 to the nearest thousand is 67,000 because the deciding hundreds digit 4 < 5. The ordering 9,000 < 90,000 < 900,000 is confirmed. These match the source's stated correct answers.

sourceClaims adjusted: the general curriculum requirement (DfE source-1 claim) was removed from activities where it supported only the topic, not the specific teaching principle; activity 3 (ordering) has no directly supporting source claim and is left as [].
Two source claims (CCSS-M 4.NBT/4.OA and NCETM/nrich) are marked unverified in the original row; their citation here is not evidence of empirical efficacy or of testing of these specific activities.

The original framing that the construction puzzle 'cannot be solved by trial alone' is softened: trial-and-error can reach the answer, but the puzzle is designed to make the place-value strategy the efficient, reasoned route.

probeDeeper: Why put the 9 in the hundred-thousands place and not in the ones?
Is 67,450 nearer 67,000 or 68,000? How do you know?
Order 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 — what do you compare first?
assess.correctAnswer: 960,000 (load the biggest digits into the highest places: 9 + 6 = 15, then zeros); and 67,000 (450 is below 500, so round down).

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't prioritise place value for magnitude — spreads the digit-sum evenly or fills low places, so the number isn't the largest (e.g. 333,300 or 111,138)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare two candidates place by place: a 9 in the hundred-thousands beats any arrangement with a smaller leading digit. Make the leading-place-dominates idea explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The number sums to 15 but isn't maximised; big digits aren't front-loaded.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the wrong way in context: 67,450 → 68,000, treating the 450 (or the 4) as enough to round the thousands up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify the decider for 'nearest thousand' (the hundreds digit): 4 < 5 so down. Place 67,450 between 67,000 and 68,000 on a line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The context answer rounds up when the decider digit (hundreds = 4) says round down.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares/orders large numbers by first digit or digit-count alone, misaligning place values
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line numbers up by place-value columns (right-aligned) and compare from the highest place down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 incorrectly, or calls a number with more digits automatically smaller/larger by looking at the wrong end.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot systematically maximise value or rounds the wrong way in context; orders by the wrong feature.
responseLevels.full: Solves multi-step large-number problems — front-loads places to maximise value, rounds correctly to a named place in context, and orders by comparing from the highest place.
responseLevels.partial: Handles single steps (rounds, or orders) but stumbles when a problem combines maximising, rounding, and comparing.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the problem and watch the reasoning: 'Make the largest six-digit number whose digits add up to 15.' Then a context item: 'A stadium holds 67,450 people — round it to the nearest thousand for a news headline.' Watch how they place digits to maximise value and which way they round in context.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'largest number' task cannot be solved by trial alone — it reveals whether the child knows value is maximised by loading the most-significant places first. The stadium item checks rounding to a named place IN CONTEXT, where children often round the visible hundreds up regardless of the thousand rule.
